name: API gateways
summary: The front door for your APIs: auth, limits and routing in one place.
howItWorks: An API gateway sits in front of backend services and handles what every API needs: authenticating callers with API keys, JWTs or OAuth, rate limits and quotas, request validation, routing paths to the right service, and usage metrics. The services behind it can focus on business logic.
analogy: Building reception. They check your badge, sign you in, cap how many visitors each company gets, and tell you which floor to go to.
useWhen: Public or partner APIs that need keys, quotas and usage plans
One entry point in front of many microservices or functions
Consistent auth and throttling without rebuilding it in every service
avoidWhen: High-volume internal service-to-service calls, where it adds latency and cost
Serving static files; that’s a CDN’s job
example: A partner integration gets an API key limited to 100 requests per second. The gateway rejects bad tokens with 401 and excess traffic with 429, and routes `/orders/*` and `/users/*` to separate services.

diagram.caption: Calls from three clients pass through the gateway. Some are rejected for bad credentials or rate limits; the rest are routed by path to the right service.

story: The idea started in the service-oriented architecture era of the early 2000s, when companies connected systems with XML web services. Rack-mounted XML appliances, such as DataPower’s (bought by IBM in 2005), sat in front of those services to secure and speed up the traffic. As public web APIs spread for mobile apps and partners, every API needed the same chores: keys, quotas, security and usage analytics. Sonoa Systems, which began with a router-like XML appliance, released Apigee in 2009 as a cloud tool for exactly that, and renamed itself after it in 2010.

Microservices made the gateway the front door to a whole system. Netflix built an edge service, Zuul, to sit between its devices and its backend services, and announced it as open source in 2013. Chris Richardson’s microservices pattern describes the result: an API gateway is “the single entry point for all clients”, which either routes a request to one service or fans it out to several.

Then gateways became products anyone could rent or download. AWS launched API Gateway in 2015, with Lambda as its headline backend; Mashape open-sourced the gateway it had built for its own API marketplace as Kong the same year; and Google bought Apigee in 2016 for $625 million.

choices.choice: Take cross-cutting chores out of every service
choices.why: Authentication, rate limits and logging are the same for every API. Doing them once at the edge keeps that code out of each service and makes the rules consistent.

choices.choice: A single entry point that can fan out
choices.why: Mobile networks are much slower and higher-latency than a data center LAN, so a screen that needs many backend calls feels sluggish. A gateway on the fast side can make those calls and return one combined reply.

choices.choice: A gateway per kind of client
choices.why: Web, mobile and partner clients want differently shaped APIs. The “backends for frontends” variation gives each its own gateway, as Netflix did with client-specific adapter code.

timeline.text: IBM buys DataPower, maker of XML gateway appliances for SOA
Sonoa Systems releases Apigee, a cloud API management tool
Netflix announces Zuul, its edge gateway, as open source
Amazon API Gateway launches; Mashape open-sources Kong
Kubernetes Gateway API reaches v1.0, a standard way to configure gateways
